questions.q: Name the three developable surfaces used to classify map projections and state the typical geometric contact (great circle, small circle, or point) for each.
questions.a: Correct answer: (1) Cylindrical – tangent along a great circle (usually equator) or secant along two small circles; (2) Conical – tangent along a small circle (standard parallel) or secant along two small circles; (3) Zenithal/Azimuthal – tangent at a point (usually a pole) or secant along a small circle. A wrong answer (e.g., "cylinder touches at a point" or "cone touches along a great circle") reveals the student confuses the dimensionality of contact: they have not visualized the 3D geometry of a developable surface touching the spheroid, a prerequisite for understanding distortion patterns in nodes 006–008.

questions.q: Explain why a conical projection is generally preferred over a cylindrical projection for mapping a country like India (extent ~8°–37°N, 68°–97°E).
questions.a: Correct answer: India's latitudinal extent (≈29°) is large but its longitudinal extent (≈29°) is similar; however, India lies entirely in the northern hemisphere mid-latitudes. A conical projection with a standard parallel near 20°–25°N minimizes distortion across the country because the cone's surface closely fits the Earth's curvature along that latitude. A cylindrical projection (tangent at equator) would place India far from the contact line, causing severe scale and shape distortion. A wrong answer (e.g., "cylindrical is better because India is rectangular") shows the student cannot link the geometry of the developable surface to the latitudinal location of the mapped region – a critical skill for selecting projections in board exam case studies.

questions.q: A map projection shows meridians as straight lines converging at a point and parallels as concentric circles centered on that point. The scale is true only along the central meridian and the standard parallel. Identify the developable surface class and whether it is a tangent or secant case.
questions.a: Correct answer: Zenithal/Azimuthal projection, tangent case (single point of contact). Steps: (1) Meridians as straight radiating lines and parallels as concentric circles is the hallmark of a planar/azimuthal developable surface. (2) Scale true only along central meridian and standard parallel indicates a single standard parallel (the point of tangency), not two standard parallels (which would be secant). (3) In a secant zenithal case, there would be two standard parallels (a small circle of contact) with true scale along both. A wrong answer (e.g., "conical secant") reveals the student cannot distinguish the graticule geometry of zenithal vs conical projections: conical also has straight radiating meridians and concentric circular parallels, but the convergence point is the apex of the cone (not the pole) and the pole appears as an arc, not a point.

questions.q: Compare the distortion distribution in a normal cylindrical tangent projection vs a normal conical tangent projection for a mid-latitude region (e.g., 30°N). Which projection would you choose for a thematic map requiring accurate area representation, and why?
questions.a: Correct answer: In a normal cylindrical tangent (equatorial contact), distortion increases with latitude as secant(φ); at 30°N, scale distortion is ~15% (1/cos30°). In a normal conical tangent with standard parallel at 30°N, distortion is zero along that parallel and increases away from it. For accurate area representation at mid-latitudes, the conical tangent is superior because an equal-area conical projection (e.g., Albers Equal-Area Conic) can be constructed with standard parallels bracketing the region, while a cylindrical equal-area (e.g., Lambert Cylindrical Equal-Area) compresses meridians severely at higher latitudes. A wrong answer (e.g., "cylindrical because it's simpler") shows the student does not analyze how distortion varies with distance from the contact line/point – a core analytical skill for node 009.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "For a world map showing ocean currents, a cylindrical projection is always the best choice because it shows the entire world in a rectangle." Provide a reasoned judgment.
questions.a: Correct answer: The statement is false. While cylindrical projections (e.g., Mercator) show the whole world in a rectangle and preserve direction (rhumb lines), they grossly exaggerate area at high latitudes (Greenland appears larger than South America), distorting the visual representation of current magnitude and heat transport. For ocean currents, an equal-area projection (e.g., Mollweide – pseudocylindrical, or Lambert Azimuthal Equal-Area for polar currents) is often better to compare current volumes. A wrong answer accepting the statement reveals the student equates "rectangular shape" with "suitability" without evaluating the projection's property preservation against the map's purpose – a key evaluation competency for board exams.

questions.q: Design a projection selection flowchart for a cartographer mapping: (a) a polar ice sheet, (b) a transcontinental highway along 40°N, (c) a global climate zone map. Specify the developable surface class and tangent/secant condition for each.
questions.a: Expected criteria: (a) Polar ice sheet → Zenithal (Azimuthal), tangent at pole (e.g., Stereographic for conformal, Lambert Azimuthal Equal-Area for equivalent). (b) Transcontinental highway along 40°N → Conical, secant with two standard parallels bracketing 40°N (e.g., Lambert Conformal Conic) to minimize scale distortion along the route. (c) Global climate zones → Pseudocylindrical equal-area (e.g., Mollweide, Eckert IV) or Interrupted Goode Homolosine; NOT a single developable surface class, but the student must recognize that no single cylindrical/conical/zenithal can adequately represent the whole world with low distortion for thematic mapping. A poor answer (e.g., "use Mercator for all") reveals the student cannot synthesize the geometric constraints of each developable surface class to match the spatial extent, location, and purpose – the ultimate synthesis skill for this chapter.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Map projection ______ by developable surface categorizes projections based on the geometric surface (cylinder, cone, or plane) that can be flattened without stretching or tearing, onto which the Earth's graticule of latitudes and longitudes is mathematically projected.
Fill in the blank: Imagine peeling an orange and trying to flatten the peel on a table – it tears because a sphere has positive Gaussian curvature and cannot be developed onto a plane without ______.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can identify the developable surface type for any named projection (e.g., Mercator = cylindrical, Lambert Conformal Conic = conical, Stereographic = zenithal), explain the geometric contact relationship (tangent vs secant) for each class, and predict the general distortion pattern (shape, area, distance, direction) associated.
